The Manage Associates page now explains what a firm is before it asks you to create one.

**What the page shows, in order**

A single white card at the top, matching the app's other Settings cards:

- **What Is a Firm?** as the card's heading.
- Three points, each with a small icon, a **bold lead-in** and its sentence:
  **Collaborate with Your Associates:** share your diary with your associates so they can add cases, update court dates, and maintain your diary on your behalf — allowing you to focus on more pressing matters.
  **Flexible Device Access:** depending on your subscribed firm plan, access your diary on 5–20 devices and invite associates up to your plan's limit.
  **Cloud Backup and Offline Access:** enjoy real-time cloud backup while retaining the ability to use your diary offline.
- A thin dividing line, then **Ready to Create Your Firm?** with your sentence beneath it. **Subscription Plans** is set bold, underlined and one size larger than the sentence around it, and tapping it opens the Subscription Plans screen already showing the **Firm** plans. The existing Create Firm section follows unchanged below the card.

The card appears for anyone who has no firm yet — whether or not they already pay — and never for a firm owner. I wrote the three bold lead-ins and the two headings in title case per the app's casing rule; the descriptions stay as ordinary sentences.

**The one change outside this section.** Subscription Plans had no way to be opened on the Firm half of the ladder, so the app opens it with a small marker in the address (`/paywall?audience=firm`). Nothing else on that screen changed — its toggle, cards, prices and buttons are as they were.

**Verified:** `flutter analyze` clean, full `flutter test` **2,103 passed**, including three new tests — the overview and its order above the name field, the link's bold/underline/larger style and the Firm marker it sends, and the plans screen opening on the Firm cards. Two existing Create Firm tests now scroll down to the form first, because the explainer pushes it below the fold on a tall phone screen — a real consequence of the page getting longer, not a test-only workaround. library;

/// Prefix of one invite's code: the invite's own id follows it.
///
/// Scoped by id rather than by firm, because an invite id is unique across firms
/// and a revoked invite's entry is removed by the same id.
const String _inviteCodeKeyPrefix = 'firm_invite_code_';

/// Reads and writes this device's remembered invite codes.
class FirmInviteCodeStore {
  /// Creates a store backed by [prefs].
  FirmInviteCodeStore(this._prefs);

  final SharedPreferences _prefs;

  /// The code remembered for [inviteId], or null when this device never had it.
  ///
  /// Synchronous on purpose: the roster's row reads it as it builds, so the code
  /// is on screen in the first frame rather than a moment later.
  String? codeFor(String inviteId) =>
      _prefs.getString('$_inviteCodeKeyPrefix$inviteId');

  /// Remembers [code] as [inviteId]'s, at the moment it is generated.
  Future<void> remember(String inviteId, String code) =>
      _prefs.setString('$_inviteCodeKeyPrefix$inviteId', code);

  /// Drops [inviteId]'s code, because the invite was revoked and nothing can
  /// redeem it any more.
  ///
  /// ponytail: a code whose invite is *used* rather than revoked stays in the
  /// preferences — the row it belonged to is gone, so nothing reads it, and the
  /// entry is a few bytes. Pruning by the live roster is the upgrade path if
  /// that ever matters.
  Future<void> forget(String inviteId) =>
      _prefs.remove('$_inviteCodeKeyPrefix$inviteId');
}

/// The one store every reader and writer shares.
final firmInviteCodeStoreProvider = Provider<FirmInviteCodeStore>(
  (ref) => FirmInviteCodeStore(ref.watch(sharedPreferencesProvider)),
);

```dart
/// The Join a Firm flow: the empty-diary test, the paying-plan warning, the
/// code window, and what is said when it succeeds.
///
/// Lifted out of `manage_associates_screen.dart` at 0.0.664 when the user asked
/// for the entry point to move to the **Firm** menu (Settings → Firm): that page
/// and the create-firm page both need exactly this flow, and neither should own
/// a copy of it.
///
/// Two rules travel with it, both user rulings:
///
///  * **Only an empty diary may join** — `join_firm` refuses an account that
///    already holds its own rows, so the count below decides whether the entry is
///    offered at all, and a count that has not arrived offers nothing.
///  * **A paying individual is warned first** that joining neither pauses nor
///    cancels their own plan; the warning's *Continue* is primary-coloured,
///    because it moves forward rather than deleting.
library;

import 'dart:async';

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:flutter_riverpod/flutter_riverpod.dart';

import '../../../core/constants/app_colors.dart';
import '../../../core/constants/app_spacing.dart';
import '../../../core/constants/app_typography.dart';
import '../../../core/errors/error_log.dart';
import '../../../core/errors/error_log_provider.dart';

import '../../../core/providers/database_provider.dart';
import '../../../sync/sync_service.dart';
import '../../auth/presentation/auth_widgets.dart';
import '../../cases/data/local/cases_dao.dart';
import '../data/account_mode.dart';
import '../data/firm_repository.dart';

/// The account's own live case count — the "empty diary" qualification for
/// joining a firm (0.0.654).
///
/// Scoped exactly as `join_firm` scopes its refusal: the rows an individual
/// holds, with no firm. A count that has not arrived yet is null, and the join
/// entry is not offered on a guess.
final ownCaseCountProvider = StreamProvider<int>((ref) async* {
  final db = await ref.watch(databaseProvider.future);
  yield* CasesDao(db).watchNonDeletedCaseCount();
});

/// Runs the join flow from whatever page offers it.
Future<void> startJoinFirm(BuildContext context, WidgetRef ref) async {
  final l = AppLocalizations.of(context);
  // A paying individual is told what joining does to their own plan before the
  // code is asked for; a free account has nothing to warn about.
  if (ref.read(premiumAccessProvider).value == true) {
    final proceed = await _confirmPlanWarning(context);
    if (!proceed || !context.mounted) return;
  }

  final redemption = await showDialog<InviteRedemption>(
    context: context,
    builder: (_) => const JoinFirmDialog(),
  );
  if (!context.mounted || redemption == null) return;
  ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(
    SnackBar(
      content: Text(
        redemption.status == InviteRedemptionStatus.alreadyMember
            ? l.auth_errorAlreadyMember
            : l.auth_joinedFirm,
      ),
    ),
  );
}
```

+/// The Join a Firm flow: who is offered it, the warning a paying individual
+/// reads first, the code window, and what is said when it succeeds.
+///
+/// It lived inside `manage_associates_screen.dart` until 0.0.664, when the user
+/// asked for the entry point to move to the **Firm** menu (Settings → Firm).
+/// Both pages need exactly this flow and neither should hold a copy of it, so
+/// the pieces live here once.
+///
+/// Two rules travel with it, both user rulings:
+///
+///  * **Only an empty diary may join.** `join_firm` refuses an account that
+///    already holds its own rows, so [ownCaseCountProvider] decides whether the
+///    entry is offered at all, and a count that has not arrived offers nothing.
+///  * **A paying individual is warned first** that joining neither pauses nor
+///    cancels their own plan. That warning's *Continue* wears the primary colour,
+///    because it is a step forward rather than a deletion.
+library;
+
+import 'dart:async';
+
+import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
+import 'package:flutter_riverpod/flutter_riverpod.dart';
+
+import '../../../core/constants/app_colors.dart';
+import '../../../core/constants/app_spacing.dart';
+import '../../../core/constants/app_typography.dart';
+import '../../../core/errors/error_log.dart';
+import '../../../core/errors/error_log_provider.dart';
+import '../../../core/l10n/generated/app_localizations.dart';
+import '../../../shared/providers/database_provider.dart';
+import '../../../sync/sync_service.dart';
+import '../../auth/presentation/auth_widgets.dart';
+import '../../cases/data/local/cases_dao.dart';
+import '../data/account_mode.dart';
+import '../data/firm_repository.dart';
+
+/// The account's own live case count — the "empty diary" qualification for
+/// joining a firm (0.0.654).
+///
+/// Scoped exactly as `join_firm` scopes its refusal: the rows an individual
+/// holds, with no firm. A count that has not arrived yet is null, and the join
+/// entry is not offered on a guess.
+final ownCaseCountProvider = StreamProvider<int>((ref) async* {
+  final db = await ref.watch(databaseProvider.future);
+  yield* CasesDao(db).watchNonDeletedCaseCount();
+});
+
+/// Runs the join flow from whichever page offers it.
+///
+/// A free account goes straight to the code window; a paying one reads the plan
+/// warning first, because joining does not pause or cancel what they bought.
+Future<void> startJoinFirm(BuildContext context, WidgetRef ref) async {
+  final l = AppLocalizations.of(context);
+
+  if (ref.read(premiumAccessProvider).value == true) {
+    final proceed = await _confirmPlanWarning(context);
+    if (!proceed || !context.mounted) return;
+  }
+
+  final redemption = await showDialog<InviteRedemption>(
+    context: context,
+    builder: (_) => const JoinFirmDialog(),
+  );
+  if (!context.mounted || redemption == null) return;
+  ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(
+    SnackBar(
+      content: Text(
+        redemption.status == InviteRedemptionStatus.alreadyMember
+            ? l.auth_errorAlreadyMember
+            : l.auth_joinedFirm,
+      ),
+    ),
+  );
+}
+
+/// The warning a paying individual reads before the code is asked for.
+///
+/// It is not ceremony: the plan is **ignored** while the account holds a firm —
+/// only the firm's expiry counts there — and the paid time stays on the account
+/// and applies again if it leaves (plan, *A Member May Not Buy A Personal Plan*).
+Future<bool> _confirmPlanWarning(BuildContext context) async {
+  final l = AppLocalizations.of(context);
+  const actionSize = Size(112, 48);
+  const actionText = TextStyle(fontSize: 16);
+
+  final answer = await showDialog<bool>(
+    context: context,
+    builder: (context) => AlertDialog(
+      title: Text(
+        l.manageAssociates_joinFirmPlanTitle,
+        textAlign: TextAlign.center,
+      ),
+      // The Invite Code window's own corner, which this screen's windows use.
+      shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(
+        borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(AppSpacing.cardRadius * 2),
+      ),
+      content: SingleChildScrollView(
+        child: Text(l.manageAssociates_joinFirmPlanBody),
+      ),
+      actionsAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.center,
+      actions: [
+        TextButton(
+          style: TextButton.styleFrom(
+            minimumSize: actionSize,
+            textStyle: actionText,
+          ),
+          onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(false),
+          child: Text(l.sharedActions_cancel),
+        ),
+        FilledButton(
+          // Primary, not red: this continues the join rather than destroying
+          // anything.
+          style: FilledButton.styleFrom(
+            backgroundColor: AppColors.primary,
+            foregroundColor: AppColors.onPrimary,
+            minimumSize: actionSize,
+            textStyle: actionText,
+          ),
+          onPressed: () => Navigator.of(context).pop(true),
+          child: Text(l.manageAssociates_joinFirmContinue),
+        ),
+      ],
+    ),
+  );
+  return answer ?? false;
+}
+
+/// The Join a Firm window: the owner's invitation code, and the two actions.
+///
+/// Built like the Invite Code window — the same panel, corner and action size —
+/// so the app's firm windows read as one family. A refusal is shown **in** the
+/// window rather than behind it, so a mistyped code can be corrected without
+/// reopening anything.
+class JoinFirmDialog extends ConsumerStatefulWidget {
+  const JoinFirmDialog({super.key});
+
+  @override
+  ConsumerState<JoinFirmDialog> createState() => _JoinFirmDialogState();
+}
+
+class _JoinFirmDialogState extends ConsumerState<JoinFirmDialog> {
+  final TextEditingController _code = TextEditingController();
+
+  bool _busy = false;
+  Object? _failure;
+
+  @override
+  void dispose() {
+    _code.dispose();
+    super.dispose();
+  }
+
+  @override
+  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
+    final l = AppLocalizations.of(context);
+    final canSend = !_busy && _code.text.trim().isNotEmpty;
+
+    return Dialog(
+      insetPadding: const EdgeInsets.symmetric(
+        horizontal: AppSpacing.md,
+        vertical: AppSpacing.lg,
+      ),
+      backgroundColor: AppColors.surfaceContainerLowest,
+      clipBehavior: Clip.antiAlias,
+      shape: RoundedRectangleBorder(
+        borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(AppSpacing.cardRadius * 2),
+      ),
+      child: SingleChildScrollView(
+        padding: const EdgeInsets.all(AppSpacing.md),
+        child: Column(
+          mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min,
+          crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,
+          children: [
+            Text(
+              l.manageAssociates_joinFirmTitle,
+              textAlign: TextAlign.center,
+              style: AppTypography.titleLg,
+            ),
+            const SizedBox(height: AppSpacing.sm),
+            Text(
+              l.manageAssociates_joinFirmIntro,
+              textAlign: TextAlign.center,
+              style: AppTypography.bodySm.copyWith(
+                color: AppColors.onSurfaceVariant,
+              ),
+            ),
+            const SizedBox(height: AppSpacing.md),
+            TextField(
+              key: const ValueKey('join-firm-code'),
+              controller: _code,
+              enabled: !_busy,
+              autofocus: true,
+              textCapitalization: TextCapitalization.characters,
+              style: AppTypography.bodyLg,
+              // The Send button reads the field, so a keystroke must rebuild it.
+              onChanged: (_) => setState(() {}),
+              decoration: InputDecoration(
+                labelText: l.manageAssociates_joinFirmCodeLabel,
+                border: OutlineInputBorder(
+                  borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(AppSpacing.radiusSm),
+                ),
+              ),
+            ),
+            if (_failure != null) ...[
+              const SizedBox(height: AppSpacing.sm),
+              Text(
+                failureText(l, _failure) ?? l.auth_errorUnknown,
+                key: const ValueKey('join-firm-error'),
+                textAlign: TextAlign.center,
+                style: AppTypography.bodySm.copyWith(color: AppColors.error),
+              ),
+            ],
+            const SizedBox(height: AppSpacing.lg),
+            Wrap(
+              alignment: WrapAlignment.center,
+              spacing: 12,
+              runSpacing: AppSpacing.lg,
+              children: [
+                TextButton(
+                  key: const ValueKey('join-firm-cancel'),
+                  onPressed: _busy
+                      ? null
+                      : () => Navigator.of(context).maybePop(),
+                  style: TextButton.styleFrom(
+                    minimumSize: const Size(112, 48),
+                    textStyle: const TextStyle(fontSize: 16),
+                  ),
+                  child: Text(l.sharedActions_cancel),
+                ),
+                FilledButton(
+                  key: const ValueKey('join-firm-send'),
+                  onPressed: canSend ? _send : null,
+                  style: FilledButton.styleFrom(
+                    backgroundColor: AppColors.primary,
+                    foregroundColor: AppColors.onPrimary,
+                    minimumSize: const Size(112, 48),
+                    textStyle: const TextStyle(fontSize: 16),
+                  ),
+                  child: Text(l.manageAssociates_joinFirmSend),
+                ),
+              ],
+            ),
+          ],
+        ),
+      ),
+    );
+  }
+
+  /// Redeems the code and closes with the server's answer.
+  ///
+  /// The membership is the server's to grant, so nothing local is written here:
+  /// the profile refresh caches the new firm and role, and the delta pull that
+  /// follows (detached, because the join has already succeeded) brings the
+  /// chamber's rows. A joining account has no rows of its own, which is why the
+  /// pull cannot overwrite anything.
+  Future<void> _send() async {
+    setState(() {
+      _busy = true;
+      _failure = null;
+    });
+    try {
+      final redemption = await ref
+          .read(firmRepositoryProvider)
+          .redeemInvite(_code.text.trim());
+      await ref.read(accountRefreshProvider)();
+      unawaited(ref.read(syncServiceProvider).syncNow(force: true, pull: true));
+      if (!mounted) return;
+      Navigator.of(context).maybePop(redemption);
+    } on Object catch (error) {
+      if (!mounted) return;
+      // Recorded here for the same reason the screen records its own: a refused
+      // code is exactly what the diagnostics log has to be able to answer.
+      recordFailure(ref.read(errorLogProvider), 'firm.join', error);
+      setState(() {
+        _busy = false;
+        _failure = error;
+      });
+    }
+  }
+}

An associate now gets a read-only view of their firm instead of only a Delete Requests card. This is recorded as **0.0.666**.

**What they see.** On Settings → Firm, an associate gets a sub menu **named after their firm** (the chamber's own name, with the line *View your firm and its associates*) where **Manage Firm** would be for an owner. It opens the same page as a read-only view: the firm identity card — logo frame and name, with no pencil and no tappable logo — and an **Associates** section listing every member of the firm with their label (Owner, Associate or Viewer), including the associate's own row. There is nothing on the page to act on: no Add Associate, no invitation codes, no permission editing, no rename, no dissolve. A failed read says so rather than showing an empty firm.

**The device card is not on it, by your choice.** You asked for Device Usage too. Its number counts the associates *plus the owner's own devices* against the plan's seats, and no member can read the owner's device count — the server hands an account only its own devices — so the card could not have been truthful. Shown that limit, you chose to leave Device Usage to the owner.

**No server work was needed.** The existing rules already let any member read their firm's own row, its roster and their colleagues' names, so this is one row on the Firm page and one read-only body on the screen. The "Only the firm owner can manage the firm" message stays as the fallback for an account whose membership details have not yet arrived, which still refuses rather than guessing.

**Yes — it means a new column on `delete_requests`** (something like `requester_name`). Today that table has no name column at all: I read its definition, and it carries `requested_by` (the UUID) plus status, note, reviewer and the sync columns, nothing more.

**Who would write it, and why that's the appeal.** The requester's own phone writes its own name as it raises the request — it does know it, because its own profile row is the one row every device has. Every reviewer's phone then receives that name in the ordinary sync, so the review shows the real name **offline, from the very first review**. Neither of the other two options can do that: option (1) only fills after the roster is read, and option (3) only works online.

**What it costs.** A Supabase migration, the regenerated SQL ledger and the schema tests (both required by your own project rules); a local database version bump, 14 → 15, with an additive column step like the last two; and the write in the create path. The sync plumbing itself needs no per-table edits — the server builds rows generically and the client rebuilds them generically, so a new nullable column rides along. Older builds simply don't write it and fall back to today's text.

**The issues, heaviest first.**

**Trust.** The name would be written by the requester's own phone, and the server's write check only verifies that the row's `requested_by` is the caller — it never looks at a name. A doctored client could therefore put *someone else's* name on a request. For a display-only line in an audit record that is low-stakes, but if you want it trustworthy the server must derive the name from the profile itself (a trigger, or the review call) rather than accept it from the client — and that is more server work than the plain column.

**It reverses a decision this app already made.** The app deliberately keeps a colleague's name off your device: that is exactly why attribution lines on cases and conflicts read *A Chamber Member*. Option (2) sends one person's name onto every member's phone and leaves it there. That is a policy change worth writing down, not just code.

**It is a snapshot, so it can disagree with the profile.** If someone renames themselves later, the request keeps the name from when it was raised. For "who asked", that is arguably the *right* answer — but it becomes a second copy of a fact that also lives in `profiles`, and the two can drift.

**It stays on the server.** Delete requests are audit history; tombstoned rows are cleared after the retention window (365 days), so the name outlives both the request and the person's membership.

**It still needs the fallback.** A requester whose own profile row has not been pulled yet — a fresh sign-in, or someone who never set a name — writes an empty name, and the reviewer sees *A Firm Member* anyway.

So: it is the most robust of the three for showing the name offline, and the most expensive and the only one that raises a trust question. If you want it trustworthy, I would have the **server** fill the name from the profile and treat the column as server-managed — that also removes the "doctored client" hole and keeps the app from being the authority on a colleague's name.

124:- **Every Member May Add And Edit, And The Shared Config Is Member-Editable (user ruling — reversed).** A newly joined associate starts with `can_add = true` and `can_edit = true`, so the chamber's cases, notes and case references are theirs to work on from the first day, with no per-member setup step for the owner to remember. **`can_delete` stays false**, because deletion inside a chamber runs through the delete-request flow, which this ruling keeps: any member may raise a request for a case, note or reference, and the owner approves or rejects it (Task 20 Phases 3–4, unchanged). The owner may still narrow add or edit per member — the toggles remain his — and **the shared config is member-editable**: the reference data (court categories, case categories, courts, steps, case types, on-behalfs) stays firm-shared under rule 10, and **every member may add, edit and reorder it** — Edit Court/Steps, case types and on-behalfs offer Add, Edit and Reorder to a member exactly as they do to the owner. The owner-only reading is **withdrawn**, on the user’s own reason: most owners do not touch cases themselves, their associates do, so a chamber in which one person alone may add a new court name or a new step queues its work behind its busiest person. Three limits hold it. **The built-in baseline is immutable for everyone:** a row with `is_custom = false` is the seeded, globally shared list, so no member and no owner may edit, reorder or delete it, and a chamber that wants different wording adds its own row. **A reference row a live case still names cannot be deleted:** refused on the device already, and the server guard is owed (see "A Reference Row A Live Case Still Names Cannot Be Deleted" below) — a tombstoned row a live case still points at would make the nightly purge fail as a whole. And **a member’s own permission still governs it:** `can_edit = false` switches their reference edits off with everything else, so the owner’s control is not lost by this reversal, only no longer the only control. Member edits are attributed (`last_modified_by`), sync like any other domain row and are visible to the whole chamber; two members changing the same court at once is an ordinary conflict on the same banner and rebase flow, because reference rows get no private path. This supersedes the shipped `join_firm` default of `can_edit = false` (`20260929102300_phase3_join_firm.sql`).
126:- **The Permission Is A Boundary, Not An Intention (user ruling).** The flags are enforced **on the server**, so a modified client — or a direct PostgREST call carrying a member’s own token — cannot name its own permissions. **INSERT is gated on `can_add` and UPDATE on `can_edit`**, read from `firm_members` for the caller and the row’s `firm_id`. **Both halves are new work** (audit correction: an earlier reading in this document called the INSERT half already enforced): there is no `can_add_firm` helper beside `can_edit_firm` / `can_delete_firm`, and `sync_can_write`’s INSERT branch reads no permission flag at all, so a member with `can_add = false` can insert a firm row through the RPC *and* straight through PostgREST today. The shape is the one the delete transition already uses — a **`BEFORE` trigger per table**, not a policy rewrite: `cases`, `case_history`, `notes`, `case_references` and the six reference tables, one trigger each, reading the caller’s `firm_members` row; `can_delete` keeps its existing gate (the delete-transition trigger plus the pending delete-request flow) and is not duplicated. **A member may not change their own flags:** the `firm_members` write path is owner-only already (`20260930210000_sync_can_write_firm_membership.sql`) and the read guard is the scoping fix below. **Per-member toggles are the only control** — one concept, not two: there is no firm-wide read-only switch, the owner who wants a frozen chamber sets every member’s `can_add` and `can_edit` off, and the owner’s own seat is not a special case to design around. Both things you saw are explained by the server's own record of what your phones sent, and the defect behind them is fixed — on the server, so the phones need no update.

**What the server logged.** For your account, the owner's phone pushed a decision on your one delete request three times at 14:37, 14:45 and 14:45 (Dhaka time) and each was refused as "not permitted" — those were the **rejections**. Each refusal made the phone undo what it had just done and show *Your Firm Permissions Changed; This Pending Action Was Not Applied.*, and the request went back into the queue — that is your "item coming back". The fourth push at 14:46 was the **approval**: the server accepted it but did **not** delete the case, because the case had been edited after the request was raised, so it asked for a reconfirm instead. That second half is the workflow behaving as designed (the queue says *Needs Reconfirmation*, the review says *This Record Changed*), not a fault.

**Why the rejection was refused.** When the app sends a decision, the server removes the "which firm" part of the row before checking whether the person may do it. Every table has a second guard to cover that, except delete requests — deliberately, so any member can raise one. So the check saw "no firm", and a reviewer's rejection, a requester's refresh and a withdrawal were all refused even though the people were allowed. The check now reads the firm stored on the request itself.

**The same flaw was refusing the firm's own edits.** With no firm visible, "may this person edit this record?" could only answer "only if they wrote it" — so an owner could not edit or delete a case or note a colleague had written. That check now sees the record as it exists, firm included. **Withdraw** also had a second blocker: the ordinary delete rule demands the delete permission, which the person raising a request never has, so withdrawing could never reach the server; a member may now withdraw their own still-pending request, and a decided one stays decided.

**Proved on your own request, without writing anything.** Two rolled-back probes through the app's own door, signed in as the reviewer: the rejection is now accepted, and the reconfirm approval is accepted *and* deletes the case, handing the tombstone back to the phone with the case's history tombstoned beside it. Afterwards the request was still parked, the case still live, and zero probe receipts — so **your next tap on Reconfirm will finish that deletion**.

**The short answer.** A delete request should be read as *"please delete this record"*, not *"delete the copy I saw"*. So when the record has already been deleted by someone else, reality has answered the request: it should close itself, leave the queue, and say so to the person who asked. It must never sit in the queue as something that can be approved but can never succeed. And when the record was edited instead, the reviewer should be confirming a deletion of **the record as it stands now** — with the current content in front of them, not the requester's older copy.

**What happens in the app today, in your exact order.** Two dependencies up front: only a member *with* delete permission deletes directly; without it, that second person's delete raises a second request instead. And the review card is drawn from the copy stored on the request ([delete_request_review_screen.dart](lib/features/settings/presentation/delete_request_review_screen.dart)).

1. A asks to delete the case. The request stores a copy of the case and the version A saw.
2. B edits the case. The case moves to a new version; **the request is untouched** — not its stored copy, not its status, and nobody is told.
3. C, holding delete permission, deletes the case. The case and its history are removed; **the request is still untouched and still says "waiting for review"**. The requester's case has vanished from the diary while their request says nothing has happened yet.
4. A reviewer opens the queue: the row is still listed, still summarised from A's original copy. Tapping Approve, the server finds nothing left to delete and answers *"The record was already deleted."* — but it leaves the request exactly as it was ([20261027130000_push_changes_check_row_firm.sql](supabase/migrations/20261027130000_push_changes_check_row_firm.sql)), so the phone applies that answer and the row **stays in the queue forever**. It can never be approved, and the only way to clear it today is to press **Reject**, which records a decision that never happened.
5. If instead the reviewer had approved *between* steps 2 and 3, the server would park it as *changed* and ask for a reconfirm. The reconfirm then deletes **B's edited version** — work the requester never saw — while the card still showed the old content. The reviewer is the safeguard there, but is being asked to confirm something they cannot see.

**The three gaps, in plain words:** a request outlives the record it names; the reviewer is asked to judge old content; and the requester is never told the record moved or disappeared. Two smaller ones sit behind them: nothing stops two members raising parallel requests for the same record, and a chosen request has no terminal state for "already gone".

**What should ideally happen.**
- **Edited:** park it as now, but show the record as it is *now*, with a plain line saying it changed after the request was raised. Reconfirm then honestly means "delete the current version", and the reviewer sees what that costs.
- **Already deleted:** close the request with "already deleted" as its outcome — reviewer and time recorded like any other decision — so it leaves the queue, stops counting in anyone's badge, and the requester's list shows that outcome instead of "waiting".
- **Requester:** their own row should say the record has changed and offer the two things they already have — refresh the copy, or withdraw. Today they learn nothing; the refresh option exists but nothing points at it.
- **Never resurrect, never re-delete:** an approval that arrives after a direct delete stays a quiet "nothing to do", and a request never brings a tombstoned record back. That part already holds.

**What it would take.** One migration (the already-deleted branch also writes a final status, reviewer and time), plus three small app changes: that status counts as decided in the queue, the status chip and the requester's badge; the review screen shows the current record beside the stored copy; and the requester's row compares the stored version with the local record to say "changed". The record lookup already exists in the view model — it is private today.

Here is the fix I propose, in plain words. Nothing below is built yet.

**1. The reviewer judges the record, not the old copy.** When a case (or note, reference, case step) is edited after the request was raised, the review screen shows **what the record says now** and keeps the requester's original copy beside it, labelled as "when the request was made". The button stays **Reconfirm**, and it now honestly means "delete this current version", because the reviewer can see what that will destroy. Today the screen shows only the old copy, and its warning even claims the details below are what exists now — which is untrue.

**2. A request whose record is gone closes itself.** The moment another member deletes the record, the request closes with the outcome "already deleted": it leaves the queue on every phone, stops counting in badges, and shows in the requester's own list as closed — not "waiting". Nobody has to press anything for that to happen. Today it stays pending forever, can never be approved, and the only way to clear it is to Reject it, which records a decision that never happened.

**3. The requester is told before a reviewer acts.** If the record was merely *edited*, their own row says the record has changed and points at the two things they already have: refresh the copy or withdraw. Today they learn nothing and the request quietly goes stale.

**4. A decision already typed on one phone is not left stuck.** If a request closes underneath a reviewer who had already staged an approval, that staged approval ends quietly against the closed request instead of becoming a conflict the person is asked to resolve.

In plain terms of cost: one small server rule (attached to the four kinds of record a request can name) plus a one-off tidy-up of any requests already left hanging, and changes to two app screens. No permission rule changes, no data removed, nothing about how deletes work for people who are allowed to delete directly.

{"kind":"tool","id":"gF8tXDEVYtg","toolName":"exit_plan","input":{"plan":"# Fixing delete requests whose record is edited or deleted by someone else

## What changes for people

1. **A request never outlives its record.** When another member deletes the case, note, reference or case step that a request names, the request closes by itself with the outcome **Already Deleted**. It leaves every reviewer's queue, stops counting in badges, and shows as closed in the requester's own list. Nobody presses anything. Today it stays "Pending" forever, can never be approved, and can only be cleared by pressing Reject — which records a decision that never happened.
2. **The reviewer judges the record, not the old copy.** When the record was *edited* instead, the review screen shows **As It Is Now** (the current values) above **When the Request Was Made** (the requester's copy), and says plainly that it changed after the request. **Reconfirm** then honestly means "delete this current version", because the reviewer can see what will be destroyed. Today the screen shows only the old copy and its warning even claims the details below are what exists now.
3. **The requester is told.** While their request is still open and the record has changed, their own row carries a **Changed** marker, and opening it says the record changed since they asked — with the two actions they already have: refresh the copy, or withdraw.
4. **An associate is warned before they edit a record that someone asked to delete.** Opening the editor for such a record shows a short window first: who asked, when, and that changing it now means the request will need confirming again. **Continue Editing** carries on; **Cancel** backs out. It warns, never blocks. It also fires when editing a note, reference or case step whose *case* has an open request, since approving that request removes them too. It is skipped for the person who raised the request (they already know).
5. **A staged decision is not left stuck.** If a request closes underneath a reviewer who had already typed an approval while offline, that decision ends quietly against the closed request instead of becoming a conflict they are asked to resolve.

## How it works

**Server — one migration, `20261028100000_delete_request_target_closure.sql`.**

- A trigger function (security definer, fixed `search_path`) runs after `is_deleted` flips false → true on the four records a request can name — `cases`, `case_history`, `notes`, `case_references`. It closes any non-deleted request for that exact row still in `pending` or `stale_review_required`, setting `status = 'already_deleted'`, `version + 1`, `updated_at` from the server clock in ms, and `last_modified_by` from the tombstone's own deleter. It is attached as an `AFTER UPDATE OF is_deleted` trigger on those four tables.
- The same migration backfills: every currently open request whose target is already tombstoned or gone is closed the same way, so nothing hangs from before the fix.
- A partial unique index (one open request per `entity_type` + `entity_id`) makes the one-at-a-time rule real. Before writing it I check the live project read-only for existing duplicates; if there are any I report them and ask rather than rewriting someone's request history.
- Why a trigger rather than an edit inside `push_changes_core`: it needs no 750-line regeneration of the push function, and it closes the request in the same transaction as the deletion, on every device, whether or not anyone opens the app. Cost on individuals: zero — no matching request exists.
- The approval path keeps working: an approval tombstones the target *before* it writes `status = 'approved'`, so the trigger's write is overwritten by the approval itself and the request still ends **Approved**. A proof asserts exactly that.

**App — four small changes.**

- `already_deleted` becomes a known status: status-chip label, and it counts as decided, so it leaves the queue and the requester's badge treats it as news. `deleteRequestNeedsReview` already excludes it.
- The review screen: `deleteRequestDetailRows` is refactored to take the entity type and a record map, so the same renderer draws both cards. A new provider exposes the target row through the existing (currently private) lookup in `DeleteRequestsViewModel`, so the screen can show the current values. The two cards appear only when the server has parked the request as stale; otherwise one card, as today.
- The requester's row compares `targetBaseVersion` with the local record's version and shows **Changed**; the actions sheet gains one explanatory line. No lookup, no marker, when the record is not on the device.
- A shared pre-edit check plus one small dialog, called before the editors open: case editor, note editor, reference editor, case-step editor. It reads the local open requests (the firm-wide read policy already grants every member those rows, so it works offline) and skips the editor's own request.

### 2026-10-28 — A request never outlives its record — COMPLETE (0.0.685)

- **What was asked.** After the 0.0.684 fix the user asked what should *ideally* happen when an associate raises a request, another associate edits the record, and a third deletes it. Three rulings were taken and all three went the recommended way — the request **survives an edit** and is reconfirmed against the newest version; a request whose record is **already deleted closes immediately**; and there is **only one open request per record** — plus a fourth instruction: **warn an associate before they edit** a record (or a step under a case) that someone else has asked to delete.
- **What was wrong.** Nothing watched the record. When a member with delete permission deleted it, the request stayed `pending` for ever: it sat in every reviewer's queue as work that could never succeed, the requester's list still said *waiting*, and the only way to clear it was **Reject** — a decision that never happened. An approval that found the record gone answered *already deleted* and left the row untouched, so it came straight back. The review screen also showed only the requester's old copy, and its warning claimed that copy was what exists now.
- **Server — one migration, applied and recorded.** `20261028100000_delete_request_target_closure.sql` adds a trigger to the four records a request may name; the moment one is deleted, every still-open request for it becomes **already_deleted** in the same transaction, stamped with who deleted it. Progress note:
Done — three changes, all on Settings → Online Sync → Sync Status.

**Header** now reads *Pending Sync* (Bengali *অপেক্ষমাণ সিঙ্ক*). Only this screen's header changed; the small sync badges that open it from the case screens and the Admin Panel keep their *Sync Status* tooltip.

**Sync Now** now runs the same forced sync the Online Sync button runs, instead of quietly scheduling one. While it works, the button greys out, shows the spinner and reads *Syncing…*; when the run returns, a toast says how it ended — *Sync Finished.* or *Sync did not complete. Your changes are safe on this device.* Those are the Online Sync screen's own two messages, and the result is read from the sync engine rather than assumed.

**Discard** was a row in each card's three-dot menu, where it could not share a button's size, background or ink. That menu contained nothing else, so it is gone: Discard is now a button beside the row's own action and takes the same black button style, size and padding as Sync Now. The confirmation window is unchanged.

One limit worth knowing: if the app refuses to sync at all — sync switched off in Online Sync, no connection, or a free plan — the engine returns without running, so the toast can say *Sync Finished.* although nothing was sent. That is exactly how the Online Sync button already behaves; that screen hides it by disabling its button in those states, and this one does not have that blocker logic.

create or replace function public.device_state()
returns jsonb
language plpgsql
stable
security definer
set search_path = pg_catalog, public
as $$
declare
  v_user uuid := auth.uid();
  v_session uuid := public.current_session_id();
  v_row public.user_devices%rowtype;
begin
  if v_user is null then
    return jsonb_build_object('status', 'unauthenticated');
  end if;

  if v_session is null then
    return jsonb_build_object('status', 'unmanaged');
  end if;

  select * into v_row
    from public.user_devices d
   where d.user_id = v_user
     and d.session_id = v_session;

  if not found then
    return jsonb_build_object(
      'status', 'unregistered',
      'cap', coalesce(public.device_cap(v_user), 1)
    );
  end if;

  if v_row.revoked_at is not null then
    return jsonb_build_object(
      'status', 'revoked',
      'cap', coalesce(public.device_cap(v_user), 1),
      'reason', v_row.revoked_reason,
      'revoked_at', v_row.revoked_at,
      'flushed', v_row.flushed_at is not null,
      'device', jsonb_build_object('id', v_row.id, 'label', v_row.label)
    );
  end if;

  if v_row.install_secret_hash is not null
     and v_row.install_secret_hash is distinct from public.current_install_hash() then
    return jsonb_build_object(
      'status', 'session_in_use',
      'cap', coalesce(public.device_cap(v_user), 1),
      'reason', 'session_in_use'
    );
  end if;

  return jsonb_build_object(
    'status', 'active',
    'cap', coalesce(public.device_cap(v_user), 1),
    'device', jsonb_build_object('id', v_row.id, 'label', v_row.label),
    'devices', public.device_list(v_user)
  );
end;
$$;

-- The rule below is the honest one: when a record a request names is tombstoned,
-- the request is answered by that fact. It becomes `already_deleted`, which is a
-- terminal state (the client reads it as a decided request, so it leaves the
-- queue and the requester is told), and the write happens in the same
-- transaction as the deletion, so every device learns it through the ordinary
-- pull whether or not anyone opens the review screen.
--

-- that function is regenerated whole by each migration that touches it, and this
-- rule belongs to the table, not to one RPC: a deletion made by any path — the
-- app's push, a direct admin edit, a future RPC — closes the request the same
-- way. The approval path keeps working untouched: an approval tombstones the
-- target *before* it writes `status = 'approved'`, so the approval's own write is

/// The service itself lives in `sync_service.dart`; this file exposes the small

import 'dart:async';

/// Re-checks this device's slot after a Realtime signal or a channel rejoin.
///
/// Deferred to a microtask so a socket callback is never re-entered by provider
/// state (a revocation signs the account out, which stops the listener). Read
/// lazily so merely building the listener does not instantiate — and claim a
/// slot with — the device gate.
void scheduleDeviceCheck(Ref ref, {required bool force}) {
  if (!ref.mounted) return;
  scheduleMicrotask(() {
    if (!ref.mounted) return;
    unawaited(ref.read(deviceGateProvider.notifier).touch(force: force));
  });
}

Done. The owner's Devices screen now shows the chamber, not just the owner's own phones.

**What the screen shows now (owner only)**
- A line across the top of the chamber's use — *4 of 5 firm devices in use* — replacing the single-account line.
- **Owner's Devices (2)** with the same rows as before, including **This device** and **Remove** for the owner's spare.
- **Associates' Devices (2)** with each associate's name, the phone's model, and when it was last used. An associate's row has no Remove, since nobody asked for that.
- Empty and failed states are stated plainly: *No associate device is signed in.*, or *Could not load your firm's devices. Pull down to try again.* with **Try Again**. An associate or individual sees exactly what they saw before.

**Why there is a server change.** The app could only ask the server about the phone in hand; the table holding every device has no read access for any client. So the owner's half had no data behind it at all. I added one read-only, owner-only function ([firm_device_list.sql](supabase/migrations/20261029100000_firm_device_list.sql)) that returns the chamber's devices with each person's name, and applied it to the live project (**79 versions**). The SQL record was regenerated, not hand-edited.

**Freshness.** The list re-reads when the screen opens and when you pull down. The same "membership changed" signal that fixes the Associates list now also drops this list, so a person who joins and signs in appears without reopening the page.

**Checks:** `flutter analyze` clean; the new SQL proof prints **FIRM DEVICE LIST OK** against the live project; [device_limit_test.dart](test/features/device_limit_test.dart) **16 passed**, including three new cases (the owner's two sections and total, an associate's unchanged list, the failed read with its retry); the migration-ledger and version-log checks pass. Version **0.0.713**.

**Two limits.** Only the **owner** sees the two sections — an associate keeps their own list. And an invited associate who has not yet signed in has no device, so they do not appear until their phone registers.

There is no mockup for this screen, so nothing in `mockup_html_screens` needed updating. Records are in [Task 12](docs/tasks/12_settings_screens.md), [the plan](docs/implementation_plan.md) and [currentlyWorking.md](docs/currentlyWorking.md).

## Google Sign-In Setup and Troubleshooting

Native Google sign-in needs two Android OAuth clients in the **same Google Cloud project as the web
client** the build passes as `GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID`, one per signing certificate, all with the package
name `com.legalcasediary.app`.

| Build | Keystore | SHA-1 | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Debug | `~/.android/debug.keystore`, alias `androiddebugkey` | `9D:8B:8E:D1:6A:52:C0:4B:B9:67:7B:C1:A2:71:3C:81:11:FD:B2:9D` | `25:21:A6:F8:81:A9:AD:52:A3:01:29:69:60:01:40:D9:78:14:0F:7A:38:FC:9D:A0:29:02:A0:A7:03:6D:04:8B` |

Re-read them at any time; the release keystore path and password live in `android/key.properties`:

```bash
keytool -list -v -keystore "$HOME/.android/debug.keystore" -alias androiddebugkey -storepass android -keypass android
```

**If sign-in fails after the account picker closes**, Android's Credential Manager reports the Google-side
configuration failure as a *cancellation*, so the sheet appears to close and nothing happens. An
instrumented run prints the tell-tale pair — a plugin line, then a `[16]` GMS code:

```text
I/PlayServicesImpl: No cancellationSignal found
I/flutter: Google sign-in failed: GoogleSignInException(code GoogleSignInExceptionCode.canceled, [16] Account reauth failed., null)
```

The app now turns that code into a visible *Google Sign-In Could Not Complete* message, so a real failure
no longer looks like a dismissal — but the cause is still server-side configuration:

- **Check the network first.** The same `[16]` appears when the request never reached Google — a Wi-Fi
  network with no uplink produces it exactly as a certificate mismatch does, and `ConnectivityMonitor`
  cannot see that case because it reports the *link*, not the internet. Google sign-in now makes a short
  request to the project before opening the sheet and reports *"No Connection. Check Your Internet And
  Try Again."* instead, so switching to mobile data is an obvious first thing to try.
- **Register the signing certificate.** Add an Android OAuth client for the SHA-1 of the build being run
  (debug, release, *and* the Google Play **App signing key certificate** from Play Console → App integrity,
  because Play re-signs uploads with its own key). A certificate mismatch is the other usual cause of `[16]`.
- **Check the package name** on each Android client: `com.legalcasediary.app`, with no typo or variant.
- **Check `GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID`** — it must be the *Web* client from that same project, and the value
  Supabase Auth is configured to trust; a Web client from another project fails the same way.
- **Publish or allowlist the consent screen.** While the OAuth consent screen is in *Testing*, every
  account that signs in must be listed under **Audience → Test users**.
- **Reproduce with the wrapper**, so the credentials are actually compiled in:
  `dart run tool/flutter_with_env.dart run -d <device>`.

# Firebase Cloud Messaging Setup — Admin Payment Notifications

A runbook for Legal Case Diary's admin notifications, written for someone who has never opened the
Firebase console. Follow it top to bottom.

This is the *other* Google console document. [google_oauth_setup.md](google_oauth_setup.md) covers
**Google sign-in**, which needs OAuth clients and does **not** use Firebase. This one covers
**Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)**, which is how an admin learns that a payment request is waiting
while the app is closed. The two share one Google Cloud project and nothing else.

> **FCM is free and needs no billing.** Google's pricing page lists Cloud Messaging as "No-cost", and
> the free *Spark* plan is enough — no credit card, no Blaze upgrade. It has throttling limits
> (600,000 messages/minute per project, 240/minute per device), not a paid allowance, so this feature
> cannot generate a bill.

---

## 1. The Mental Model (Read This Once)

| Party | What it is | What it does here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The payer's app** | Any signed-in phone | Inserts a row into `payment_submissions` when it submits a TrxID |
| **The database** | Supabase project `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` | A trigger calls an Edge Function, which reads the pending count and the admin device tokens |
| **FCM** | Google's push transport | Delivers one small message to each admin's phone — including while the app is closed |
| **The admin's app** | The APK on the admin's phone | Turns that message into one local notification, worded from the app's own ARB files |

Three consequences worth knowing before you start:

- **The phone never opens a connection.** FCM uses the one persistent connection Android already
  keeps for all apps, which is exactly why Android recommends it over an app holding its own socket.
  The message handler only posts a notification — it makes no network call, opens no database.
- **The notification's words live in the app, not on the server.** FCM carries *numbers*
  (`{"pending": "3"}`), and the app writes the sentence from `app_en.arb` / `app_bn.arb`. That is what
  keeps Bengali correct per device and keeps every visible label in the ARB files.
- **`google-services.json` is not a secret.** Google ships it inside every APK. It is git-ignored here
  for the same reason `env.json` is — it is a build input naming one Firebase project — not because it
  is sensitive. The **service-account key** in §6 *is* a secret and never leaves Supabase.

---

## 2. The Values You Will Need (Copy From Here)

| Name | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Google Cloud **project number** | `38386857573` (the project that already holds the Web client `…g0bkds`) |
| **Firebase project id** | `legalcasediary-17985` — the id paired with that number; the key in §6 and the send endpoint are built from it |
| Android **package name** | `com.legalcasediary.app` |
| Supabase project | `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` (**never** the other project) |

**Use the project you already have.** Do not create a new Google Cloud project for Firebase: the
project number above is the one whose Web client Supabase trusts for sign-in.

---

## 3. Step 1 — Add Firebase To Your Existing Google Cloud Project

1. Sign in to <https://console.firebase.google.com> with the **one** account that owns the project.
2. Click **Create a project** (the button reads that even when you intend to reuse one).
3. On the first step, choose **Add Firebase to an existing Google Cloud project** — a link or a
   dropdown near the project-name field — and pick the project whose number is `38386857573`.
   Only projects that do not already have Firebase are offered, so if the list is empty, the project
   already has Firebase and you can skip to §4.
4. Continue through the steps. **Analytics is not needed** — decline or remove Google Analytics if the
   wizard offers it. Nothing in this feature uses it.

If a wizard ever insists on creating a *new* project, stop: two projects would mean an FCM
configuration that does not match the sign-in clients, and this document's values would no longer
apply.

---

## 4. Step 2 — Register The Android App

1. On the project overview, click the **Android** icon (**Add app → Android**).
2. **Android package name**: `com.legalcasediary.app` — exactly, or FCM will not deliver.
3. **App nickname**: `Legal Case Diary`.
4. **Debug signing certificate SHA-1**: *leave it empty.* FCM does not use it — the SHA-1 is what
   Google sign-in matches against, and
   [google_oauth_setup.md §7](google_oauth_setup.md#7-step-3--create-the-android-clients) already
   registered those clients. Entering it here can raise the console's *"the Android package name and
   its fingerprint are already in use"* error, which is expected and does not need resolving.
5. Click **Register app**.

---

## 5. Step 3 — Put `google-services.json` In Place

Download the file the console offers (`google-services.json`) and save it as:

```text
android/app/google-services.json
```

It is git-ignored, so every machine that builds for Android — yours, and the CI runner — needs its own
copy. The google-services Gradle plugin
([`android/settings.gradle.kts`](../android/settings.gradle.kts)) turns it into the resources the
Firebase SDK reads, and a build without it fails rather than shipping an app whose push is silently
dead.

For CI, encode it and store it as the repository secret `GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON_BASE64`
(GitHub → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):

```bash
base64 -w0 android/app/google-services.json
```

Open the file and check `project_info.project_id` — the **Firebase project id**, which is what the send
endpoint in §6 is built from. This project's id is `legalcasediary-17985`, paired with the number above;

`package_name` of `com.legalcasediary.app`. If the package name differs, the app was registered wrong
— delete it in Firebase (**Project settings → Your apps**) and repeat §4 rather than editing the file
by hand.

=== token repo ===
/// The device's push registration: its row in `device_tokens`.
///
/// Classified **local operational** (Rev 2.4 table classes): per-device state the
/// client writes about itself. It is never synced, never firm-shared, never
/// tombstoned, and legitimately **hard**-deleted, because a device unregisters
/// itself on the way out of an account. The table, its self-only policies and its
/// `on delete cascade` to `auth.users` are the whole of
/// `supabase/migrations/20261012120000_admin_payment_alerts.sql`.
///
/// **The row's `user_id` is never taken from a caller.** RLS admits a row only for
/// `auth.uid()`, so the id this repository writes is the signed-in account's own,
/// read from the client — a caller-supplied id could only ever be refused. The
/// token is the primary key, so re-registering updates the row rather than adding
/// a second one, and a device that changes hands is reassigned to its new account
/// instead of continuing to feed the previous one.
library;

import 'package:supabase_flutter/supabase_flutter.dart';

/// Where this device's push registration lives.
abstract class DeviceTokenRepository {
  /// Upserts [token] for the signed-in account.
  ///
  /// Idempotent: the same device signing in again rewrites its own row.
  Future<void> register(String token, {String? deviceKey});

  /// Removes [token].
  ///
  /// The way a device stops receiving alerts for an account: it runs on every
  /// sign-out, before the session ends, while the row is still its own to delete.
  Future<void> unregister(String token);
}

/// Talks to the `device_tokens` table under the caller's own RLS.
class SupabaseDeviceTokenRepository implements DeviceTokenRepository {
  /// Creates a repository over [client].
  SupabaseDeviceTokenRepository(this._client);

  final SupabaseClient _client;

  @override
  Future<void> register(String token, {String? deviceKey}) async {
    final userId = _client.auth.currentUser?.id;
    if (token.isEmpty || userId == null) return;
    await _client.from('device_tokens').upsert(<String, Object?>{
      'token': token,
      // The account's own id, from the session rather than an argument.
      'user_id': userId,
      // Which device holds this token, so a revocation can delete exactly
      // this device's row rather than the whole account's.
      if (deviceKey != null && deviceKey.isNotEmpty) 'device_key': deviceKey,
    }, onConflict: 'token');
  }

  @override
  Future<void> unregister(String token) async {
    if (token.isEmpty) return;
    await _client.from('device_tokens').delete().eq('token', token);
  }
}

/// The inert repository of a build with no backend.
///
/// A device with no Supabase project has nothing to register with, and saying so
/// silently is better than a row that could never be written — the same choice
/// `UnavailableAdminRepository` makes about the panel.
class UnavailableDeviceTokenRepository implements DeviceTokenRepository {
  /// Creates the inert repository.
  const UnavailableDeviceTokenRepository();

  @override
  Future<void> register(String token, {String? deviceKey}) async {}

  @override
  Future<void> unregister(String token) async {}
}

**Commit it.** For this project the ignore rule is costing more than it protects.

**Why committing is right here**
- It is not a secret, by construction. It contains a project number, project id, an app id, an OAuth client id and an API key — and every one of those already ships inside every APK you build. Anyone with your app on their phone can extract it. Git visibility changes nothing about exposure; it only changes convenience.
- The file is a *build input that must match the applicationId*. That is exactly the kind of fact that belongs in version control. After the rename, the `package_name` inside it and the `applicationId` must both move together; as a tracked file, that is one visible diff. As an ignored file, it is an invisible local file that can silently disagree — which is precisely the confusion we just spent a round on, where the file sat in a checkout whose branch had no FCM code at all.
- Your CI does extra work only because the file is hidden: a base64 secret, a write step, a JSON validation step, and a build that fails with a custom error when the secret is missing. Committing deletes all four moving parts, and a fresh clone builds without a manual step.
- You have one Firebase project and no flavors. Ignoring is the right call when `google-services.json` differs per environment — staging vs production, debug vs release — because then committing one would force every developer onto the same project. That is not your situation, and if it ever becomes one, you add flavors and ignore per-flavor files then.

**The one thing to fix regardless:** in Google Cloud, restrict the API key in that file to Android apps — package `com.legumsoft.legalcasediary` (and the current one until the old build is dead) plus the debug and release SHA-1s. That is what actually protects the key; git visibility is not the control. If the key were unrestricted, it would be worth fixing today whether the file is committed or not.

**What "commit" means concretely.** Remove the `android/app/google-services.json` entry and its comment from `.gitignore` on `BugFix-Supabse`, stage the file, and simplify `release.yml` by dropping the `GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON_BASE64` write/validate step (the repository secret can be deleted afterwards). Then update the two comments that describe it as ignored — `build.gradle.kts` and the FCM setup doc — so the next reader is not told the opposite of what the repo does.

**The one argument for keeping it ignored**, stated fairly: if you ever want the same source tree to build against two Firebase projects, a tracked file blocks that and you will be reintroducing flavors or a generate-from-template step. You would also be publishing your project id and app id in a public repository — harmless, but it does invite random traffic against the FCM endpoint if the sender ever accepts unauthenticated calls. Neither applies today.

So: commit it, delete the CI secret plumbing, and keep the API key restricted to your package and certificates.

A client *ID* is an immutable identifier: nothing in Google Cloud renames it. The entry's **name** (the label in the console) is editable, and an Android client's package-name field can be edited in the console's edit view — but Google's own documentation only covers creating, deleting and restoring clients, not changing the package on an existing one, so that path is undocumented and can take five minutes to a few hours to propagate. Given the cost of the safe route is two minutes, use it: **create two new Android clients** with `com.legumsoft.legalcasediary` and the same SHA-1s, then leave or delete the old pair. Nothing in the app references those client IDs — the build only ever passes the **Web** client ID as `serverClientId` — so new IDs require no code change and no Supabase change. If you edit the old clients in place, the only real consequence is that the old package stops matching, which is what you want anyway; it is simply the less predictable of the two.

**2. Firebase — no new service account, no new private key.**

The service account is a property of the **Google Cloud/Firebase project**, not of the Android app inside it. Your sender builds its endpoint from `project_id` (`legalcasediary-17985`) and signs with the existing key stored as Supabase's `FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`; neither of those values changed when the package changed. A new private key would be needed only if you created a *new* Firebase project, deleted or rotated that service account, or its key was lost. Just confirm the two anchors in the file you downloaded: `project_id` is still `legalcasediary-17985`, `project_number` is still `38386857573`, and it now contains a client whose `package_name` is `com.legumsoft.legalcasediary`. If it still lists only the old package, the Android app was not added to the same Firebase project and the build will keep saying *No matching client found*.

**3. "Re-encode the CI secret" — the release workflow otherwise builds with the old file.**

`android/app/google-services.json` is git-ignored, so the GitHub Actions release job cannot see your local copy. It recreates the file from the repository secret `GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON_BASE64` before building. Your new file means that secret is now stale, and a tagged release would fail with the same "no matching client" error. To update it:

```bash
base64 -w0 android/app/google-services.json
```

Copy the single-line output, then GitHub → repository **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → `GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON_BASE64` → Update**, and paste it. That is the whole step; the workflow decodes it and validates the JSON itself. Local builds need none of this. If you instead decide to commit the file (what I recommended earlier), the secret and that workflow step become unnecessary — but until you do, the secret must be refreshed or the CI build is dead.

**Short answer: remove the two old Android IDs, keep the Web client ID first, and add nothing else.** Keeping them would not break anything, but they now name clients tied to the old package, so they are stale configuration that will mislead you during the next debugging session.

Why that is safe, precisely:

- **Supabase only checks the token's audience.** The app builds the Google token with `serverClientId` set to the Web client ([supabase_auth_repository.dart:538-540](lib/features/auth/data/supabase_auth_repository.dart#L538-L540)), so every token Supabase ever receives is addressed to the Web client. A token addressed to an Android client is never produced by this app — not by the old build either, since it also passed the Web ID as `serverClientId`.
- **The Android clients only satisfy Play Services**, matching package name and signing certificate before the account sheet appears. They are never transmitted to Supabase, so listing them there was never load-bearing. The codebase has no browser OAuth call (`signInWithOAuth`) either, which is the one flow where a listed client's redirect URI would matter.
- **A dead string in that list is inert.** Supabase does not validate the entries against Google when you save; an unused entry just sits there. Deleting one only means a token with that audience would be refused — and none exists.

So the field should read, in this order:

1. the **Web** client ID (unchanged, must stay first),
2. optionally the two **new** `com.legumsoft.legalcasediary` Android IDs — harmless as documentation, functionally unnecessary.

If you keep only the Web ID, Google sign-in behaves identically. The one mistake to avoid is putting an Android ID in front of the Web ID, or replacing the Web ID with one: that is exactly the mismatch that produces *Unsupported provider* / audience errors at sign-in. Save the field and sign in once with Google to confirm.

Also note the old Android client IDs stay valid identifiers in Google Cloud until you delete those clients — deleting the clients does not retroactively break anything in Supabase, but if you want the Supabase field to reflect reality, clean the IDs out in the same sitting.

docs/implementation_plan.md:374:  - **Deleting the data without the account, and no SQL to do it (0.0.473, user request).** Two more cards join the **Danger Zone** directly above **Delete Account**, and the account's plan picks which is drawn: **Delete Local & Cloud Data** for a premium account, **Delete Local Data** for a free one. Both are the same `SettingsActionCard` as Delete Account (destructive tone, its own subtitle, its `busy` spinner while the run is in flight), both open the **one** tick list — **Cases**, **Notes**, **Case References** and **Custom Seed Data** (the court categories, court names, steps, case types and on-behalfs the user added, named in that row's supporting line) — and both remove **only** what was ticked, leaving the profile, the subscription and the settings alone. The confirm is disabled while nothing is ticked, and a dismissed window deletes nothing: the pop-over **is** the confirmation (the user chose no second typed gate). **There is no new server SQL and no second delete path.** Every row goes through the repository that already owns its delete (`LocalCaseRepository.deleteCase`, the notes and reference repositories, and the court-category, court, step, case-type and on-behalf repositories), so a deletion here is built from the same soft delete, the same `sync_queue` entry and the same offline compaction matrix as a delete from a case card — a row that never reached the server has its pending insert **dropped** rather than queued as a delete the server would refuse as an unknown id, and a pushed row is queued as a **tombstone**. The premium card then runs `runBacklogPush` (the engine's own gate: no client, offline, sync switched off or not entitled all refuse without sending anything), which is what carries the tombstones to Supabase — so a second device learns of the deletion and `purge_tombstones()` removes the rows after 365 days, exactly as for any other delete. **Decided with the user:** the cloud copy goes through that normal path rather than a new hard-delete RPC (no migration to write, and another device still holding the rows cannot re-upload what this one removed); Custom Seed Data removes **only** `is_custom` rows and never the built-in baseline every install reads; a **firm** account is refused with a sentence, because its diary is shared with colleagues; and the premium card **refuses while offline** rather than queueing the account's half for later. **What is deliberately kept:** `case_notification_preferences` (a per-user preference class the request keeps, and the notification job only alerts for cases that still exist), and `delete_requests` / `conflict_log` (a request queue and a rejected-mutation log, not the user's own data — and the firm case that could hold a request is refused wholesale). **Order and safety:** cases are deleted before the reference data, so a run that ticks both frees the custom court those cases pointed at; with Cases unticked, a custom court or on-behalf a **remaining** case still names — and a custom category any live row still names — is **kept**, because deleting it would leave a row pointing at a reference this device no longer holds; and the whole deletion is **one transaction**, so a refusal (the extended-offline recovery lock) leaves every row exactly where it was and reports its own failure sentence. The card is chosen from a **known** plan — only `premiumAccessProvider == true` gets the cloud card — because the smaller promise is the one that can never take away a copy the user did not ask to lose, and the free card's work is local, so it needs no link at all. Pinned by `test/features/data_deletion_test.dart` (12 cases: what each tick removes, the tombstone against the dropped insert, the baseline that survives, the row held back because a case still names it, the push reported as sent or as pending, and the rollback) and seven cases in `manage_account_test.dart` (which card is the plan's, the disabled confirm, ticking one kind and leaving the rest, a dismissal, the firm refusal, the offline refusal, and the cloud card deleting locally with the account's copies queued). **(0.0.474, user request)** The user reversed the no-second-gate decision: the tick list's red button now opens a typed confirmation screen (`DeleteDataConfirmScreen`), where `delete my data` must be typed before anything is destroyed — one new ARB key (`settingsManageAccount_deleteDataConfirmPhrase`, English in both languages like `delete my account`), compared trimmed and case-insensitively, back is a cancellation. The same pass paints both warnings' destructive actions red-background/white-text and sets the Danger Zone label 1px bigger (13px, still bold error). **(0.0.680, user request) The two windows are cut like the Exit App window, and the seed row's tick rides its title.** The **Delete Account** warning and the **Delete Data** tick list now wear the Exit App window's `shape` — a `RoundedRectangleBorder` at `BorderRadius.circular(AppSpacing.cardRadius * 2)`, that window's 8 px — instead of Material's default corner, so every destructive window on Manage Account reads as one family. In the tick list, the **Custom Seed Data** hint was the tile's `subtitle`, which made that row the only two-line tile in the list and left its tick centred against the tile — level with the hint rather than with the title above it. The hint is now a `Text` **under** the row, its left edge pinned to the title's, so every row is a single-line tick and every tick rides its own title; `ListTileTitleAlignment.titleHeight` was tried first and left the tick 4 px low, which the measurement caught, hence the construction rather than the flag. The row's key moved from the tile to the whole row so it can be measured as one. Nothing else moved: the same four ticks, the same two gates, the same deletion, no server work. Pinned by `manage_account_test.dart` — *the two destructive windows share the Exit App corner* (teeth proved: with the shape left default it fails, `Expected: BorderRadius.circular(8.0)`, `Actual: BorderRadius.zero`) and *the seed row's tick rides its title, not its hint*, which measures the tick's centre against the title's, the hint's top against the title's, and the hint's left edge against the title's.

 - **0.0.260** — The FAB now asks which kind of note to create: **Text Note** (the Phase 1 flow, unchanged) or **To-Do**, whose body is Google Keep's checklist — a tick, an editable item and a remove button per row, plus an **Add Item** row, with Enter on a row opening the next. Ticking an item drops it below the unticked ones (Keep's own rule, applied as a stable partition) and strikes it through; unticking lifts it back into the unticked block. A new to-do opens with one empty row ready to type into, and blank rows are dropped on save. This is a deliberate extension of the plan's `notes` schema (§ `notes`, which defines `title` + `body` only): `notes.items` holds the checklist as a JSON `[{text, done}]` array, and `null` there means a text note — so a note's kind is the presence of that column rather than a second flag to keep in step. `body` mirrors the item texts, one per line, which is what keeps the plan §12.1 title+body search able to find a to-do by its contents with **no query change**. A to-do card shows its first three rows with their ticks and `+N More`, so the two kinds read differently at a glance. **Part B must carry `items` on the server `notes` table**; the local sync payload already does. Files: `notes_table.dart`, `note_items.dart` (new), `note_detail_screen.dart`, `notes_screen.dart`, `notes_repository.dart`; schema v9 + `from < 9` migration. Tests: `test/features/notes_todo_test.dart` (13).
 
 - **0.0.202** — Both libraries' search box now behaves exactly like the case-list one, because it is the same box in the same place: `ScopedSearchBar` is mounted by `CasesScreenModal` (under the header, above the scrolling list) instead of being the first row of the notes/reference `ListView`. It used to scroll away with the cards, sit inside the list's 16 px padding, and vanish entirely when the library had no rows — an empty library could not be searched at all. The screens pass `isSearching` / `searchController` / `onSearchChanged` to the modal and `_NotesList` / `_ReferenceList` lost the controller, the search callback and the `onCloseSearch` they no longer need. Note/reference filtering, the header search icon, the always-on (x) and tap-outside-to-hide-the-keyboard are unchanged. (`notes_screen.dart`, `case_reference_screen.dart`; tests: `test/features/library_search_test.dart`, 3.)

Pinned by `library_search_test.dart` (*the Add Case Reference title band is the app black*). The `caseReference` mockup was updated to match (rule 9).
 - **0.0.700** — An existing note or to-do opens **read-only**, and **Edit** sits to the right of **Delete** (user request). The detail page starts in a view state: the title and body `TextField`s are `readOnly` with no cursor and no input hint, a to-do's ticks are wrapped in `IgnorePointer` (so they keep their normal colours but do not change), and its **Add Item** and per-row remove buttons are not built. /// One law (Act, Ordinance or Statute) a case reference may cite.

```dart
  /// Creator of a custom law; null for pre-seeded rows.
```
